{{Short description|Statistical property}}
'''Lexicographic dominance''' is a [[total order]] between [[random variable]]s. It is a form of [[stochastic ordering]]. It is defined as follows.<ref name=":02">{{Cite book |last1=Chakrabarty |first1=Deeparnab |last2=Swamy |first2=Chaitanya |title=Proceedings of the 5th conference on Innovations in theoretical computer science |chapter=Welfare maximization and truthfulness in mechanism design with ordinal preferences |date=2014-01-12 |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1145/2554797.2554810 |series=ITCS '14 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=105–120 |doi=10.1145/2554797.2554810 |isbn=978-1-4503-2698-8|s2cid=2428592 }}</ref>{{Rp|page=|pages=8}} Random variable A has lexicographic dominance over random variable B (denoted <math>A \succ_{ld} B</math>) if one of the following holds:

* A has a higher probability than B of receiving the best outcome.
* A and B have an equal probability of receiving the best outcome, but A has a higher probability of receiving the 2nd-best outcome.
* A and B have an equal probability of receiving the best and 2nd-best outcomes, but A has a higher probability of receiving the 3rd-best outcome.
In other words: let ''k'' be the first index for which the probability of receiving the k-th best outcome is different for A and B. Then this probability should be higher for A.

== Variants ==
'''Upward lexicographic dominance''' is defined as follows.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Cho |first=Wonki Jo |date=2016-01-01 |title=Incentive properties for ordinal mechanisms |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0899825615001608 |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |language=en |volume=95 |pages=168–177 |doi=10.1016/j.geb.2015.12.003 |issn=0899-8256|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Random variable A has upward lexicographic dominance over random variable B (denoted <math>A \succ_{ul} B</math>) if one of the following holds:
* A has a ''lower'' probability than B of receiving the ''worst'' outcome.
* A and B have an equal probability of receiving the worst outcome, but A has a lower probability of receiving the 2nd-worst outcome.
* A and B have an equal probability of receiving the worst and 2nd-worst outcomes, but A has a lower probability of receiving the 3rd-worst outcomes.

To distinguish between the two notions, the standard lexicographic dominance notion is sometimes called '''downward lexicographic dominance''' and denoted <math>A \succ_{dl} B</math>.

== Relation to other dominance notions ==
First-order [[stochastic dominance]] implies both downward-lexicographic and upward-lexicographic dominance.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Cho |first1=Wonki Jo |last2=Doğan |first2=Battal |date=2016-09-01 |title=Equivalence of efficiency notions for ordinal assignment problems |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0165176516302476 |journal=Economics Letters |language=en |volume=146 |pages=8–12 |doi=10.1016/j.econlet.2016.07.007 |issn=0165-1765|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The opposite is not true. For example, suppose there are four outcomes ranked z > y > x > w. Consider the two lotteries that assign to z, y, x, w the following probabilities:

* A:   .2, .4, .2, .2
* B:   .2, .3, .4, .1

Then the following holds:

* <math>A \succ_{dl} B</math>, since they assign the same probability to z but A assigns more probability to y. 
* <math>B \succ_{ul} A</math>, since B assigns less probability to the worst outcome w. 
* <math>A \not\succ_{sd} B</math>, since B assigns more probability to the three best outcomes {z,y,x}. If, for example, the value of z,y,x is very near 1, and the value of w is 0, then the expected value of B is near 0.9 while the expected value of A is near 0.8. 
* <math>B \not\succ_{sd} A</math>, since A assigns more probability to the two best outcomes {z,y}. If, for example, the value of z,y is very near 1, and the value of x,w is 0, then the expected value of B is near 0.5 while the expected value of A is near 0.6.

== Applications ==
Lexicographic dominance relations are used in [[social choice theory]] to define notions of [[strategyproofness]],<ref name=":0" /> incentives for participation,<ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Aziz |first=Haris |date=2016-11-08 |title=Participation Incentives in Randomized Social Choice |class=cs.GT |eprint=1602.02174 }}</ref> [[Ordinal Pareto efficiency|ordinal efficiency]]<ref name=":1" /> and [[envy-freeness]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cho |first=Wonki Jo |date=2018-06-01 |title=Probabilistic assignment: an extension approach |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00355-018-1110-z |journal=Social Choice and Welfare |language=en |volume=51 |issue=1 |pages=137–162 |doi=10.1007/s00355-018-1110-z |s2cid=19700606 |issn=1432-217X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Hosseini and Larson<ref name=":12">{{Cite book |last=Hadi Hosseini, Kate Larson |title=Strategyproof Quota Mechanisms for Multiple Assignment Problems |date=2015-07-24 |oclc=1106222190}}</ref> analyse the properties of rules for [[fair random assignment]] based on lexicographic dominance.
